# Testing Whether SAE Feature Labels Generated by LLMs Are Faithful or Confabulatory

**Problem:** A common practice is to automatically label SAE features by passing their top-activating examples to an LLM (e.g., GPT-4) and asking it to describe the common theme. However, LLMs are known to confabulate plausible-sounding descriptions even when given incoherent inputs. If the LLM labeler finds a theme in a truly polysemantic feature, the resulting label creates a false appearance of monosemanticity—a failure mode that makes SAE features appear more interpretable than they actually are.

**Direction:** Using SAELens on GPT-2 small, select 40 features: 20 high-frequency and 20 low-frequency features. For each, generate an LLM label by passing the top-10 activating examples to GPT-4o-mini and asking for a one-sentence description. Then create a 'shuffled control': for each feature, randomly shuffle the top-10 examples between features to create incoherent input sets. Re-label these shuffled sets. Have human raters score both the original and shuffled labels for coherence (1–5). If shuffled labels score nearly as high as original labels, this demonstrates LLM labelers confabulate apparent coherence on incoherent inputs.

**Why it matters:** If automated SAE feature labeling is unreliable, a large fraction of interpretability results in the literature may be labeling artifacts. This would call for mandatory human validation of SAE feature labels in any safety-relevant application.

**Relevant context:** Automated feature labeling via LLMs is standard practice in papers using Neuronpedia and SAELens. The concern about LLM confabulation in labeling has been mentioned anecdotally but not systematically tested. CE-Bench (2025) proposed contrastive evaluation approaches, indicating the community acknowledges the labeling reliability problem.
